items.text: The dependency research (desktop-release-control-plane-audit) is completed and provides a comprehensive map of the 4-system pipeline. Key input: version records are split across 3 systems with incompatible ID schemes (integer profile versions, git commit hashes, semver release versions). The audit identified 7 gaps, several of which (git commit traceability, version sync callback) directly feed into the schema this research must define.

LPBS already has git_commit_hash on download_artifacts (added via migration in main.go:806). The Go struct DownloadArtifact includes GitCommitHash, ReleaseVersion, Platform, IsCurrent, SHA256/SHA512, and timestamps. This means the cross-system correlation key (git commit) is already storable in LPBS — the gap from the audit is partially closed at the schema level, though population through the pipeline needs verification.

'Profile version' (deployment-manager integer counter for config snapshots) and 'release version' (LPBS semver for customer-facing artifacts) are fundamentally different lifecycle tracks. The unified model must treat them as separate concepts that happen to coexist in the same release flow, not try to merge them into one version number.

items.topic: Where should the canonical 'release record' live?
items.context: Currently no system records the full release event (version + commit + platform + channel + timestamp + who approved). The record could live in deployment-manager (which owns approval and orchestration), LPBS (which owns published state), or as a new shared concept. Each choice has different tradeoffs for queryability and system coupling.

options.label: deployment-manager owns the release record
options.rationale: DM already orchestrates releases and owns approval state. Adding a 'releases' table here keeps the audit trail next to the approval chain. LPBS stays focused on artifact storage/serving. Downside: DM must be queried to know what's live, even though LPBS is the actual publisher.

options.label: LPBS owns the release record
options.rationale: LPBS is the source of truth for published state. Adding a release history table here means 'what's live' and 'what was live' are in the same system. Downside: LPBS would need to know about approvals and deployment context it currently doesn't have.

options.label: Both systems get release records (event-sourced via webhook)
options.rationale: LPBS fires a publish webhook (already a planned gap fix), DM records the event. Each system has a release record optimized for its queries. Downside: two sources of truth, eventual consistency concerns.

items.topic: What should the canonical release identifier be?
items.context: A release record needs a stable ID that can be referenced across systems. Options range from using existing IDs (git commit hash, LPBS artifact ID) to minting a new dedicated ID. The choice affects how systems reference releases and how history is queried.

options.label: Composite key: (app_key, platform, variant_key, release_version)
options.rationale: Uses existing LPBS identifiers. Uniquely identifies a release in customer terms. Downside: verbose, and release_version alone isn't unique across platforms/channels.

options.label: UUID minted at release time by the orchestrator
options.rationale: A single opaque ID that all systems can reference. Clean for cross-system joins. Downside: requires the orchestrating system to mint and propagate the ID.

options.label: Git commit hash as primary correlation key
options.rationale: Already flows through all 3 systems. Natural for provenance queries. Downside: one commit can produce multiple releases (different platforms/channels), so it's not unique per release.

items.topic: Should the model include a formal channel promotion concept?
items.context: Currently channels (variant_key in LPBS) are flat — 'stable' maps to 'default', and there's no relationship between channels. Some products use a promotion model (nightly → beta → stable). Defining this now would shape the release record schema (e.g., 'promoted_from' field). Leaving it out keeps the model simpler but may require a breaking change later.

options.label: Yes — define channel ordering and promotion semantics now
options.rationale: Future-proofs the schema. Enables automated promotion pipelines. Adds complexity to the initial model.

options.label: No — keep channels flat, add promotion later if needed
options.rationale: Simpler initial model. Current usage only has 'stable'. YAGNI until there's a concrete multi-channel product.

items.text: deployment-manager's existing 'deployments' table records execution logs with JSONB 'artifacts' but does NOT record the resulting release_version, platform, or channel of what was published. The version sync callback (audit gap #7) would need to populate these fields — either by extending the deployments table or creating a new 'releases' table.

items.topic: Scope: Should customer-visible release history (changelog, release notes) be part of this model?
items.context: LPBS download_assets already has a release_notes TEXT field. The research description mentions 'customer-visible release history.' This could mean just the data model for what customers see, or it could extend to a changelog API, release announcement system, etc. Scoping this affects how much schema design is needed.

options.label: Include release notes in the release record, but no separate changelog API
options.rationale: The release record captures notes alongside version/platform/channel. Changelog display is a UI concern built on top of the record. Keeps the model focused.

options.label: Design a full changelog model with structured entries
options.rationale: A proper changelog has categories (features, fixes, breaking changes), per-version grouping, and rendering rules. More complete but significantly more scope.

options.label: Exclude customer-facing content entirely — focus only on internal record structure
options.rationale: Keeps the research tightly scoped to IDs and references. Release notes and changelogs are a separate concern.

items.text: LPBS ListArtifactsByApp (download_hosting.go:939) already returns artifacts with is_current flags per (app_key, platform), providing a basic version history view. However, this is artifact-centric (binary files) not release-centric (semantic events). A release record would add: who approved it, when it was promoted, which deployment triggered it, and correlate artifacts across platforms into a single 'release.'

plan_updates: Created conclusion.md scaffold with research question, methodology, and 5 initial findings: incompatible version ID schemes, profile vs release version distinction, implicit-but-not-queryable history, underspecified channel model, and missing release event record.
